description:
Hello! I am a Physics major currently enrolled in college, and am interested in space and astronomy. I am always interested in learning, and hope to grow enough to overcome hardships.

For this team, the project, centered on the Lunar Landing Site, we are attempting to build the framework for a webpage or application that simplifies information gathered about the Moon's terrain and gives it to the user in a quickly understand fashion.
summary: To attempt to find a solution for the challenge proposed, we worked primarily on two separate functions of the application we planned to put together. First, on the visual end, we used Unity and Moon terrain height map data to create a representation of the Moon as viewed from an observer. For the second part, we used Python in Visual Studios Code to interpret two CSV files that had been manually placed into folders by the user, resulting in arrays that show Sun and Earth visibility from a location on the Moon, as well as the intensity of sunlight on that location over time. While not connected currently, we plan to combine the two aspects of the application into one, as well as add features to allow for automatic data collection from the NASA webpages, given a user-inputted time range. By showing intensity of the sun, we can estimate how much power could be generated at each location, and by showing the visibility of the Earth, it can be determined whether radio communication between Earth and Moon is possible.
details: Using Unity and a height map converted to a format readable by Unity, a 3D terrain map of the Moon was created and could be explored by moving the camera around through directional keys. Additionally, the Unity program included a solar panel, settings for the solar panel to automatically face the Sun for optimal light gathering, manual sliders for tilt and rotation of the solar panel, and a test output for power generated by the sunlight on the panel. This map also could be configured to use a moon rock texture found online from a Unity Assets webpage, but was not used in the final project. The second part was coded in Python using VS Code, and took in select data from two CSV files gathered from Horizons and Quickmap, outputting an array containing a timestamp (relative to data range start), the expected intensity of sunlight on the solar panel, and a boolean value telling us when the Earth was visible. Additionally, by inputting the current time in days since start of data range, it could be determined when the next sunset and Earthset would occur, if the range included their setting. By changing the path variables at the top, different files could be selected. We currently lack code that would alter the intensity of sunlight for when the Sun is only partially obstructed, and we would like our application to gather the data automatically to fit user needs, rather than drawing it from folders that have to be filled manually.
